title: Checking a claim before you share it
essentialQuestion: How can you find out if a story is true before you share it?
learningGoal: Use lateral reading to check a made-up news story against other sources, and decide whether to share it.

warmUp.question: A friend sends you a surprising story. What do you do first?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does the post say? What do the other sources say?

cases.name: Brightwater Daily Truth
cases.body: “BIG NEWS. The Brightwater bridge closes for a WHOLE YEAR from tomorrow. Share this before they delete it.” There are no names, and no link to the town council.

False. The bridge closes for two days, not a year.

activity.title: Read sideways
activity.instructions: Here is a post about the Brightwater bridge. Before you decide, open the other sources one at a time, like a fact-checker opening new pages. Then answer the question. You can open them in any order.

sections.heading: Ask three questions before you share
sections.text: Messages can spread very quickly, and a shocking story often travels fastest. In Brightwater, a page called Brightwater Daily Truth posted that the town bridge would close for a whole year. The post used capital letters and said, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like these push people to hurry, and hurrying makes it easy to share something false. Before you share, ask three questions. Who is behind the information? What is the evidence? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post gives no names, no evidence and no link to the town council, which looks after the bridge.
sections.simpler: Messages spread fast. Shocking stories spread fastest. A page in Brightwater said the bridge will close for a year. It said, “Share this before they delete it.” Words like this make you hurry. When you hurry, you can share something false. So first, ask three questions. Who is behind it? What is the evidence? What do other sources say? The Brightwater post has no names. It has no evidence.

sections.heading: Read sideways, like a fact-checker
sections.text: Researchers once watched how different people checked websites. Students, and even history professors, stayed on one page and read it carefully from top to bottom. A page that looked official often fooled them. Professional fact-checkers did something different. They left the page quickly and opened other sources to find out who was behind it and what others said about it. This is called lateral reading, which means reading sideways across many sources instead of down one page. The fact-checkers reached better answers in much less time. In the activity, you can read sideways too, by opening the Brightwater sources one at a time.
sections.simpler: Researchers watched people check websites. Students read one page from top to bottom. So did history teachers. A page that looked real often fooled them. Fact-checkers did something else. They left the page fast. They opened other sources. They found out who made the page. This is called lateral reading. It means reading sideways, across many sources. The fact-checkers got better answers, and faster.

sections.heading: Decide what to share
sections.text: When several trusted sources agree, a claim is more likely to be true. The town council, the local radio news and a fact-checking group all say the bridge will close for two days of repairs, not a whole year. So the first post is false, even though it looked exciting. If a claim is false, don't share it. If you want to help, share the council's notice instead. Sometimes you can't check a claim, for example when there is no internet. Then you can ask a teacher or someone who knows, or simply wait. A story that is true will still be true tomorrow.
sections.simpler: Do many trusted sources agree? Then the claim is more likely true. The council says the bridge closes for two days. The radio says two days. The fact-checkers say two days. So the first post is false. Don't share a false claim. Share the notice from the council instead. Sometimes you can't check, like when there is no internet. Ask a teacher, or wait. A true story is still true tomorrow.

glossary.definition: Something a person says is true. It may be true or false.
glossary.example: “The bridge closes for a whole year” is a claim.

glossary.definition: Facts or proof that show if something is true.
glossary.example: The council notice gives the dates of the repairs. That is evidence.

glossary.definition: The person or place that information comes from.
glossary.example: The radio news is one source about the bridge.

glossary.definition: A person whose job is to find out if claims are true.
glossary.example: The fact-checkers said the post about the bridge was false.

glossary.definition: Checking a page by looking at what other sources say about it.
glossary.example: Lateral reading showed that the bridge closes for two days.

checks.question: What did the fact-checkers do differently?

options.text: Read every word on the page slowly
options.feedback: Not quite. That is what the students and professors did. Read the second section again.
Yes. They left the page and read sideways across other sources. This is lateral reading.
Not quite. A false page can have good pictures. Read about what the fact-checkers did.

checks.question: Three trusted sources say the bridge closes for two days. What should you do with the first post?

options.feedback: Yes. The post is false. You could share the council's notice instead.

options.text: Share it so people can decide
options.feedback: Not quite. Sharing a false post helps it spread. Read the third section.

options.text: Share it, because it might be true
options.feedback: Not quite. Three trusted sources say it is false. Read the third section.

write.prompt: A friend wants to share the Brightwater bridge post. Explain how you checked it, and what you would tell your friend.
sentenceStarters: Then I read sideways. The ___ said ...
So I think the post is ...
selfCheck: I used at least one of the three questions.
I said what two other sources say.
I said what my friend should do.
write.example: First, I asked who is behind the post. The post had no names, no evidence and no link to the council. Then I read sideways. The council notice said the bridge closes on 3 and 4 May for repairs. The radio news said the same, and the fact-checking group said the post is false. So I think the post is wrong about the whole year. I would tell my friend not to share it, and to share the council's notice instead.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner reads the Brightwater post aloud. You ask the three questions, and your partner answers from the lesson. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud what lateral reading means, and how a fact-checker uses it.

watch.title: Sort Fact from Fiction Online with Lateral Reading
watch.why: It comes from the group that studied the fact-checkers in this lesson. It explains lateral reading.
watch.beforeQuestion: How do you decide if a website can be trusted?
watch.afterQuestion: How is reading sideways different from reading down one page?
watch.summary: This short video explains lateral reading. It is a way to check information that professional fact-checkers use. Many people check a website by reading down the page. They look at how it looks and what it says about itself. But a page can look serious and still give false or one-sided information. Fact-checkers do something different. After a quick look, they leave the page. They open new pages and search for what other sources say about it and about who is behind it. By reading less of the page and more about it, they learn more, and they learn it faster. You can do the same thing. Before you trust a page, find out who made it and what others say about it.
keyPoints: One page can fool you, even if it looks serious.
Fact-checkers leave the page and read what other sources say about it.
Find out who is behind the information before you trust it.
watch.contentNote: Fast American English, made for secondary school. It shows searching online, which learners on an offline device can't do; the activity's source cards stand in for new pages. The summary was written from the Digital Inquiry Group's own description and the research it is based on, not from watching it, and the length is not confirmed. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Use only harmless, made-up stories. Don't use real rumours about sensitive topics such as legal processes, aid, resettlement or official services, which can be too close to home. If a learner raises one, don't debate the details; point them to the official organisation that runs that service.
educatorNotes: This builds on Our World Lesson 23 (What makes information trustworthy?), which teaches source, date and context. This lesson adds lateral reading. If a class uses both courses, start by recalling Lesson 23's checks.

Lateral reading normally needs the internet. On an offline device the activity's source cards stand in for new pages; in class, a teacher can play “the other sources” on paper. In Indonesia, Mafindo recommends fact-checking sites such as TurnBackHoax and CekFakta (Liputan6, 2026).
